question: What makes the fast dance feel like a release from the slow opening?
intro: A measured, declamatory Lassan gives way to a dance-like Friska, then delays its conclusion before the final rush. Martha Goldstein’s performance lets the contrasts of pulse, register and density carry a piece often reduced to its most familiar tune.

cues.title: A declamatory beginning
cues.text: The Lassan begins with a weighty, speech-like manner before the faster dance arrives. Listen to the gaps around the phrases as well as their accented notes: the opening’s flexibility establishes a strong contrast for what follows.
cues.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._2 describes Lassan and Friska. Analysis places the first substantial sounding windows after a short lead-in, around 0:05–0:10.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Follow the phrase not a metronome
cues.text: In the slow span, attend to how each gesture gathers and releases its weight. A flexible declamatory phrase can remain coherent without making every small subdivision equally prominent.
cues.evidence: General listening prompt for the Lassan; no measured tempo or particular rubato is asserted.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Ornament and arrival
cues.text: The Lassan places decorative movement around a more deliberate melodic outline. Try hearing the points towards which the ornaments move, rather than giving every rapid note the same structural weight.
cues.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._2 describes the Lassan’s character and contrasting minor/major regions. This is a general textural account.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A published Hungarian rhapsody
cues.text: Liszt writes this rhapsody in 1847 and publishes it in 1851, dedicating it to Count László Teleki. Its sequence of contrasted characters belongs to a written concert work, even when the piano suggests an improvising ensemble.
cues.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._2 gives composition, publication and dedication.

cues.title: Different colours within the Lassan
cues.text: The slow half does not remain in one expressive colour. Listen for a melody or accompanying pattern to retain its identity as register, weight and harmonic surroundings change.
cues.evidence: General listening suggestion; the source describes contrasts within the Lassan, but individual chords are not inferred from machine key estimates.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Renewed weight within the slow span
cues.text: A stronger passage follows the preceding quieter material. Compare its declamatory weight with the beginning while retaining the slower section’s larger scale; this is not yet the final fast dance.
cues.evidence: Analysis boundary 2:54, then stronger windows at 3:10–3:15; the sustained Friska onset is much later, around 6:12.

cues.title: The bass gives gestures direction
cues.text: Throughout the slow half, listen below the ornaments for the bass notes that support each gesture. A change of foundation can redirect a phrase even when its upper line remains recognisable.
cues.evidence: General piano-texture prompt for the Lassan, not a timed chord identification.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A late Lassan crest
cues.text: This late part of the slow section reaches a marked rise in recorded level, then retreats. Hear the crest in relation to the long opening half, rather than assuming that the first strong climax must begin the Friska.
cues.evidence: Analysis: −17.8 dB at 4:15 rises to −11.2 at 4:25 and −11.9 at 4:30, then −29.3 by 4:40.

cues.title: Romani performance and Hungarian style
cues.text: Liszt’s Hungarian idiom draws on popular and urban repertories mediated by Romani performers. It is not the same enterprise as the later collection of rural folk song by Bartók and Kodály; “Hungarian” here names a historically specific concert language.
cues.evidence: The site Liszt biography distinguishes popular melodies and Romani performance from later ethnographic folk-song collection.

cues.title: The slow half releases its hold
cues.text: The Lassan’s final withdrawal makes room for the change of character. Listen through the thinning sound and the space before the next sustained movement; the fast half does not need to announce itself at maximum volume.
cues.evidence: Analysis: −21.9 dB at 5:50 falls to −42.5 at 6:00 and −55.6 at 6:10, followed by renewed attacks from 6:15.

cues.title: The Friska starts to move
cues.text: The fast section begins lightly enough for its repeated patterns to gather momentum. Listen for a more regular dancing pulse to emerge from the freedom of the Lassan, rather than for an immediate wall of sound.
cues.evidence: Analysis: new activity after the quiet 6:10 window, onset density around 3.2 at 6:15; sustained rise through 6:40–7:10. Work form places the Friska after the Lassan.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Repetition gains force
cues.text: The repeated pattern becomes stronger across this span. Small changes in register, accent and harmonic support can intensify a dance without replacing its rhythmic identity.
cues.evidence: Analysis level rises from −22.1 dB at 6:40 to −12.1 at 7:00 and −9.6 at 7:10. General textural explanation does not assign individual attacks.

cues.title: Two different rhythmic jobs
cues.text: Separate the tune from the quicker repeated accompaniment. Their rhythms need not coincide at every instant: the lower pattern can keep the dance moving while the upper line stretches across it.
cues.evidence: General Friska listening prompt; analysis also shows sustained higher onset density around 7:20–8:10.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The dance accumulates weight
cues.text: This stretch builds towards another strong crest while the dancing motion continues. Compare the accumulation with the Lassan’s more isolated declamations: sustained repetition now carries much of the energy.

cues.title: A Goldstein performance
cues.text: The Commons file names Martha Goldstein and traces the recording to the Al Goldstein collection at ibiblio. It does not establish a session date or instrument make; those details remain open rather than being borrowed from another Goldstein recording.
cues.evidence: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Franz_Liszt_-_Second_Hungarian_Rhapsody.ogg — author, source and embedded album metadata.

cues.title: Changing figures the same dance
cues.text: The later Friska sustains rapid activity while changing the shape of the figuration. Keep the underlying dance in mind when an ornament, leap or repeated-note pattern briefly becomes the most conspicuous feature.
cues.evidence: Analysis high onset density around 9:35 and 9:45–10:00; general prompt, not identification of a particular figure at 9:30.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A pause in the drive
cues.text: The recorded level withdraws substantially after the busy dance span. Listen for the changed sense of continuity: the approach to the ending allows more space and contrast instead of merely continuing to accelerate.
cues.evidence: Analysis: −16.3 dB at 10:00, −26.6 at 10:05 and −37 at 10:20; boundary 10:26.

cues.title: Room for a cadenza
cues.text: Liszt permits a cadenza before the final Prestissimo. Listen for the contrast between this freer late passage and the preceding regular dance.
cues.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._2 documents the cadenza ad libitum. Analysis boundaries 10:26–11:04 and reduced levels support a contrasting late span; its edition and authorship are unestablished.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Listen across the freer span
cues.text: In the late passage, follow the larger gestures through the changing density rather than trying to maintain the earlier dance pulse unchanged. The interruption makes the eventual restoration of regular motion more consequential.
cues.evidence: Analysis shows lower levels and strongly varying onset densities across 10:30–12:10. No exact cadenza boundaries or written bars are claimed.

cues.title: The final drive approaches
cues.text: The freer span yields to renewed activity and a rise in force. Listen for the restored dance character to gather the music into its final stretch rather than opening another long slow episode.
cues.evidence: Analysis strongest boundary 12:14; −29 dB at 12:10, −21.8 at 12:15, then −8.7 by 12:30.

cues.title: An emphatic major ending
cues.text: The written destination is F♯ major, not the C♯ minor of the Lassan’s main argument. The last strong gestures turn the dance’s energy into a closing statement, then leave room for the piano’s final decay.
cues.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Rhapsody_No._2 gives the final F-sharp-major cadence. Analysis peaks late near 12:45, then falls to −41.2 dB at 13:00 and silence by 13:05.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The slow argument renews its contrasts
transitions.how: Within the Lassan, changing register and harmonic colour renew the declamatory material after a quieter interval. The contrast remains inside the slow half: a local increase of force is not yet the release into the regular dance of the Friska.
transitions.evidence: Analysis boundary 2:54 and renewed stronger span around 3:10–3:15. No individual modulation is inferred from the audio key labels.

transitions.title: The Lassan releases the fast dance
transitions.how: The slow span withdraws into a deep reduction of level before renewed repeated patterns establish the Friska. The faster dancing pulse grows from a relatively light beginning, making the change of rhythmic character more important than an immediate increase to maximum force.
transitions.evidence: Analysis: near-silence around 6:10, renewed attacks from 6:15 and gradual increase through 7:10; Lassan/Friska design documented by the work source.

transitions.title: The dance gives room to freer gestures
transitions.how: After the sustained dance, the texture becomes less continuous and the dynamic scale contracts. The score allows a cadenza before the final Prestissimo, setting freer gestures against the preceding regular dance.
transitions.evidence: Analysis boundary 10:26, with further changes at 10:38–11:04 and lower levels through 12:10; source documents the optional cadenza.

transitions.title: Freer gestures restore the final dance
transitions.how: The freer late passage yields to renewed regular motion and increasing force. The final dance directs the rhapsody towards its F♯-major close; the renewed energy functions as a conclusion rather than another full cycle of slow and fast sections.
transitions.evidence: Analysis strongest boundary 12:14, late level rise through 12:30–12:45; the written final cadence is later in the closing span.

composer.born: 22 October 1811, Doborján, Kingdom of Hungary (now Raiding, Austria)
composer.epithet: The touring pianist who made a single theme change character, and eventually stripped virtuosity down to a few unresolved notes.
facts: Piano with Carl Czerny and composition with Antonio Salieri in Vienna; later composition with Anton Reicha in Paris
Weimar masterclasses; first president of the Hungarian Royal Academy of Music, founded in 1875
Piano music and transcriptions; thirteen symphonic poems; two programme symphonies; concertos, songs and sacred music
composer.background:
Liszt was born in Doborján, a German-speaking village in the Hungarian kingdom, where his father Adam worked on an Esterházy estate. Hungary remained his declared homeland, although German and French were his principal languages. Adam taught him piano before taking him to Vienna in 1822 for lessons with Carl Czerny, who had studied with Beethoven, and Antonio Salieri. The family moved to Paris the following year. The Conservatoire refused him admission as a foreigner; private teaching and public concerts supplied his education instead. His early career therefore joined two institutions that would remain distinct in his adult life: the disciplined lesson and the commercial concert platform.

Adam died in 1827, leaving the sixteen-year-old Liszt to support himself and his mother by teaching. Paris offered an education beyond the keyboard: Victor Hugo, the religious social thinker Félicité de Lamennais, Chopin and Berlioz belonged to his intellectual or musical circle. Hearing Paganini in 1832 suggested that a pianist might make technical difficulty carry the same theatrical force as the violinist’s leaps and harmonics. Liszt responded with prolonged practice and transcription: his piano version of Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique, published in 1834, aimed to preserve orchestral detail.
